newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian dlr in holding pattern, Kiwi dlr dives.
newsitem.headline: Australian dlr in holding pattern, Kiwi dlr dives.

text.p: The Australian dollar barely twitched against its U.S. counterpart Monday, holding the tight pattern set during last week's indecisive trading.

The risk of another rate cut here remained the dominant factor, as it has virtually every day for the last two months. Some dealers felt the market had already priced in the event, written a post-mortem and moved on to future policy prospects.
Now all it needed was for reality to catch up.
What movement there was came on the crosses where it made early gains on the mark and Swiss franc, but suffered a late dip in sympathy with the Kiwi which hit a fresh 1-1/2 year low.
By 4.45 pm (0645 GMT) the dollar had glided to US$0.7360/65 from an early US$0.7374/79, having closed at US$0.7404/09 Friday after failing to sustain a rally to US$0.7425 resistance.
The latter barrier was expected to cap the currency short term while support under US$0.7330 had proved solid last week leading dealers to conclude a rate cut was fully priced in.

It had held around US$0.7380 for most of the session but dipped in late trade when the Kiwi crumbled 1/2 cent to its lowest level since December 1995. It was reacting to comments from New Zealand finance minister Bill Birch that the Kiwi was likely to fall further as the RBNZ eased policy.
Late in the day the Kiwi had sunk to US$0.6435/40 from US$0.6520/27 at the start of the day and also lost ground on the Australian dollar to NZ$1.1422/42 from NZ$1.1312/22 late Friday.

The A$ followed the U.S. dollar higher against the mark in the morning to almost make a six year high, as interest rate differentials and expectations of a soft European single currency drove investors elsewhere.

Late profit-taking eroded the gains but still left it firm at 1.3571/03 marks and 1.1188/03 francs from 1.3582/04 and 1.1199/22. It was steady on the yen at 86.20/30 yen from 86.11/21 and unchanged on its trade weighted index at 57.6.
Despite the late slip dealers felt last week's 18-month low around US$0.7310 was well protected by bids beneath US$0.7330 and would hold until the Reserve Bank's intentions on rates became clearer.

A 50 basis point cut in official rates to 5.0 percent was largely priced in following two months of steady selling from 78 cents, but other outcomes were possible and the market was taking no chances.
Most expected the bank to move the day after its monthly board meeting on August 5 and felt the dollar could rally even if it did ease by the 50 basis points expected.
If August 6 passed with no move, the market would begin to wonder if all the speculation had been in vain and the easing cycle actually ended with the last cut on May 23.
Such a development could see the dollar bounce sharply, although the RBA has caught the market by surprise enough times in the past to keep buyers cautious.
Data this week included the balance of goods and services, building approvals and retail trade, but none should impact on rate expectations unless well outside forecasts.
The June trade balance on Tuesday should show the largest surplus ever but only thanks to accounting of the RBA gold sale.

The Bureau of Statistics plans to account for the RBA's sale of its gold reserves as exports and, since 125 tonnes of gold were sold forward for June delivery, analysts are expecting a surplus of anything up to A$2.2 billion.

That would be way up on May's A$873 million, which itself was boosted by the sale of a A$500 million frigate, and imply a hefty contribution to Q2 GDP from net exports. But the effect of the gold sale on GDP would be largely negated as it implied a corresponding fall in stocks which would detract from GDP.
Building approvals for June are seen down 1.5 percent but that should not alter the outlook for a steady housing recovery.
The retail trade figures on Thursday could stir some market activity given how volatile the series has been this year.

The median forecast is for a sober 0.4 percent rise in June following the steep 2.9 percent gain in May, but estimates range from a rise of 1.5 percent to a fall of 1.5 percent. Figures on real sales for the quarter should show an increase of just 0.1 percent against 2.2 percent in Q1.
Analysts felt it would take a jump in June sales of more than 2.0 percent to make the market reconsider its rate cut assumptions.
-- Wayne Cole 9373 1800
